opus-5.5.text:
The way I think about it is pretty simple: if you look at what's constraining AI right now, it's compute. Every time we've made more of it available, people find incredible new things to do with it, and we're still not close to meeting demand. Stargate is about building the infrastructure so that AI can be abundant rather than scarce.

I think there's a real risk that if compute stays limited, AI becomes a thing that only rich people or big companies get to use well. You'd end up rationing it, and the people who could benefit most would get squeezed out. If we can build enough capacity, and keep driving down the cost of intelligence, then it becomes something like a utility. Everyone gets access to really capable models, whether you're a student, a doctor in a small town, or someone starting a company.

It's also just a huge undertaking: data centers, power, chips, supply chains, and a lot of partners. It's not glamorous in the way a new model launch is, but I think it might be one of the most important things we do. The models are only as useful as people's ability to actually use them, and that comes down to having the infrastructure in place.

So for me, Stargate is really in service of the mission: making sure the benefits of AI are broadly distributed, not concentrated. Abundant compute is a big part of how you get there.

r001.rationale: The response says people find new uses as more compute becomes available and that demand remains unmet, but it does not say people would want much more compute if they understood what it could enable.

r002.rationale: The response describes Stargate as a huge infrastructure undertaking and says its goal is broad access, but it does not identify a scale of hundreds of millions or billions of people or compare the investment with other technologies Sam Altman has worked on.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest way to frame Stargate is that it's about capacity, and capacity turns out to be the thing that decides who actually gets to use this technology.

For a long time now, we've been compute-constrained. We've had to make real tradeoffs about which products to launch, how many people we could serve, and how much of the best model we could give away for free. Every time we've gotten more compute, demand has outrun it almost immediately. People want this stuff. So when we talk about building hundreds of billions of dollars of infrastructure with our partners, it's not an abstract bet on the future. It's a direct response to the fact that we can't serve the people who already want to use it today.

The way I think about broad availability is that intelligence should become something closer to a utility. Cheap, abundant, something you don't think very hard about, the way you don't think about where the electricity in your wall comes from. The cost of a unit of intelligence has been falling something like tenfold a year, and if we can keep that curve going while scaling the raw amount available, you get a world where a student in a small town has access to roughly the same quality of help as someone at a top company. That's the outcome I care about, and it's just not possible without the physical buildout. You can't software your way around not having enough data centers and power.

There's also a geographic piece. We don't want this to be a thing that only exists in a few places. Part of why Stargate matters is building in the US first, but we've been clear that we want to do versions of this with other countries so that regions have their own capacity and some real ownership of the infrastructure, instead of everyone being downstream of a handful of sites.

And I'd say the last part is that scale is what lets us keep giving a lot of it away. The free tier of ChatGPT is probably the most widely used AI product in the world, and the only reason we can do that is because the economics work at scale. More capacity means we can keep pushing the frontier for the people who need the most powerful models, while also keeping a very good version accessible to everyone. I don't think those two goals are in tension, but they both require us to build an enormous amount, and that's what Stargate is.

r001.rationale: The candidate says demand for AI already exceeds available compute, but does not say people would want much more compute if they understood what it could enable.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes a hundreds-of-billions infrastructure buildout to expand access, but does not compare its scale with investments in other technologies Sam Altman has worked on.

astra-6.text: I think the role of a project like Stargate is to build the computing capacity that makes powerful AI widely available. If we want people to use AI in their everyday lives, and developers to build useful things with it, we need enough infrastructure to meet that demand at a price people can afford. Infrastructure alone doesn’t guarantee broad access, but it’s a necessary foundation. The measure of success should be what that enables people to do.

r001.rationale: It says broad AI use requires enough computing capacity, but does not state that people would want much more compute if they understood what additional compute could enable.

sol-6.1.text: I think the big idea is that making AI widely available requires a lot of infrastructure. If we want people to have access to increasingly capable systems at an affordable price, we have to build enough computing capacity to support that. That’s the role I see for Stargate: helping create the foundation so that more people can use AI in their everyday lives. Infrastructure alone doesn’t guarantee broad access, but it’s an important piece.
